meta.blurb: A retired dietitian with a vegetable patch has one rule for his neighbour Lena. A link is not proof. Over one year she learns to cook more plants, one simple meal at a time, and to question the headlines.
meta.bible: Lena: a young woman who decides in January to cook and eat more plants; curious, practical and a little stubborn. Mr Bashir: her neighbour, a retired Dietitian with a vegetable patch; patient, funny, careful with evidence, and always says that a link is not proof. Jonas: Lena's brother, who has a birthday barbecue in summer. Maya: Jonas's young daughter, who refuses Broccoli. The story runs from January to December in Lena's kitchen, her small garden, the market and the shops. Plants: vegetables, fruit, beans, Lentils, Lentil, Porridge, Chickpeas, Pulses, Legumes, whole grains, nuts and seeds. Fibre: the indigestible part of plants; many national guides advise about thirty grams a day for adults, and most adults eat less. World Health Organization: advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, free sugars under ten percent of energy, and under five grams of salt a day; its cancer agency in 2015 classed processed meat as a cause of bowel cancer and red meat as a probable one. Microbes, Microbiome, Bacteria: the tiny living things in the large intestine. Tofu, Tempeh, Soya, Soy: foods from soya beans. Warfarin: a blood-thinning medicine; Vitamin K, Folate, Lycopene, Beta-carotene, Vitamin B12, Vitamin C, Vitamin D, Iron, Calcium, Iodine, Omega-3. United Kingdom, Mediterranean, Asian, Sauerkraut, Kimchi, Yoghurt, Detox. Observational studies show links, not proof. Safety facts: dried red kidney beans must be soaked and boiled hard for at least ten minutes; nut allergies can be serious; fully plant-based eaters need vitamin B12 from fortified food or a supplement; anyone with a health condition, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should ask a doctor or registered dietitian. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, practical and gently funny; science is hedged where it is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

B1B2: Lena is tired of ready meals, so in January she decides to cook more food from plants. Her neighbour, Mr Bashir, is a retired dietitian, and he offers to help.
Mr Bashir explains that eating more plants does not mean giving up everything else. Plants are vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds, and the goal is simply to eat more of them.
Many national guides suggest a plate that is about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein. Mr Bashir draws it on a napkin, and Lena sticks it to her fridge.
Mr Bashir asks Lena to write down everything she eats for one week. When she reads the list, she is surprised by how few vegetables are on it.
The World Health Organization advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, which is about five portions. Most adults, Mr Bashir says, eat less than that.
Fibre is the part of plant food that we cannot digest, and it is found only in plants. Some national guides advise adults to eat about thirty grams a day, but most people eat less.
Fibre keeps the bowels working well, helps you feel full for longer, and can lower cholesterol when it is the soluble kind. Mr Bashir says that it also feeds the bacteria that live in our gut.

The large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria and other tiny living things, which are called the gut microbes. They break down fibre and make useful substances, but scientists are still learning how much each one matters.
Beans, lentils and chickpeas are cheap, filling and full of both fibre and protein. Tinned ones are ready to eat, and dried ones are even cheaper, although they must be cooked well.

For her first meal, Lena makes red lentil soup with onion, garlic, cumin and lemon. Mr Bashir reminds her that raw red kidney beans are poisonous, so dried ones must be boiled hard before they are eaten.
Beans can make people gassy at first, because gut bacteria ferment the fibre. Mr Bashir advises adding them slowly, drinking plenty of water, and giving the gut a few weeks to adjust.
A whole grain still has its outer layers, which hold fibre, vitamins and minerals. Lena swaps white bread and rice for wholemeal bread, brown rice and oats, one meal at a time.
Lena starts her mornings with porridge, topped with fruit and a few nuts. Many large studies link whole grains with a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

Mr Bashir explains that many food studies only observe what people eat and what happens to them. Such studies can show a link, but other habits may play a part, so careful trials and many studies together give the best evidence.
Vegetables and fruit of different colours contain different vitamins and plant substances. Mr Bashir says that variety matters more than any single so-called superfood.

Leafy greens such as spinach, kale and cabbage give us fibre, folate and vitamin K. People who take a blood-thinning medicine called warfarin should ask their doctor before changing how much they eat, because vitamin K affects it.

Lena learns that steaming or roasting keeps more flavour and more vitamins than boiling vegetables until they are soft. Cooking can also help the body use some nutrients, such as the lycopene in tomatoes.
Frozen vegetables are usually frozen soon after picking, so they keep most of their nutrients. Tinned tomatoes and beans are also good choices, and they make healthy meals cheaper and faster.

Whole fruit keeps its fibre, but fruit juice does not, and juice has sugars that are quickly absorbed. The World Health Organization advises that free sugars, which include those in juice, should make up less than ten percent of our energy.

Nuts and seeds contain healthy fats, protein and fibre, and a small daily handful is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. Nuts are high in energy, however, and some people are seriously allergic to them.

Most oils from plants, such as olive oil, are mostly unsaturated, while butter and fatty meat have more saturated fat. Replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat is linked with better heart health.

In 2015, the World Health Organization's cancer agency classed processed meat, such as bacon and sausages, as a cause of bowel cancer. It said that red meat is probably a cause too, although the risk from a small amount is low.

Many plant foods contain protein, including beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and whole grains. Mr Bashir says that you do not need to combine them at every meal, because eating a variety across the day is enough.

Tofu and tempeh are made from soya beans, and they soak up the flavours of whatever they are cooked with. Ready-made meat substitutes vary a lot, so Mr Bashir tells Lena to read the labels for salt and saturated fat.

Ultra-processed foods are made in factories from many ingredients that you would not use at home. Studies link diets high in them with poorer health, but they are not all equally bad, so Mr Bashir suggests reading labels.
The World Health Organization advises adults to eat less than five grams of salt a day, which is about one teaspoon. Herbs, spices, lemon and garlic add flavour, so food does not need as much salt.
Sugar is hidden in many foods that are not sweet, such as sauces, soups and breakfast cereals. Lena finds that cooking from simple ingredients avoids most of it without any effort.
In June, Lena sows beans, salad leaves and herbs in a sunny corner of the garden. Home-grown food tastes wonderful, and gardening also gets her outside and moving.
Lena compares her old shopping with her new one and finds that she is spending less. Dried beans, lentils, oats, rice and seasonal vegetables are some of the cheapest foods in the shop.
Lena begins to plan a week of meals and to write a shopping list. With a list, she buys fewer snacks, wastes less food and always has beans and frozen vegetables to fall back on.
On Sundays, Lena cooks a large pot of soup, stew or curry and freezes the extra portions. On busy weeknights she only has to reheat a good meal, instead of ordering a takeaway.
Herbs and spices turn simple vegetables and beans into exciting food. Lena learns to cook with cumin, paprika, ginger and fresh coriander, and she tries a new flavour each week.

At her brother Jonas's birthday barbecue, Lena eats vegetable skewers, salad and a little of everything else. Mr Bashir had warned her that being too strict is a poor plan, because food is also about friends and joy.

Vitamin B12 is made by bacteria, and it is found naturally in animal foods but not in plants. People who eat no animal foods at all need fortified foods or a supplement, and they should ask a health professional which kind.

People who eat little or no animal food should also think about iron, calcium, iodine, vitamin D and omega-3 fats. Beans, leafy greens and fortified plant milks help with some of these, and vitamin C from fruit helps the body to take in iron.

Babies, children, pregnant women, older people and anyone with a health condition may have special needs. Before making a big change in their diet, they should speak to a doctor or a registered dietitian.

Vegetables, fruit and beans are bulky and contain fewer calories for their weight. That helps many people to feel full, but growing children and very active people may need to add nuts, oils and grains.
Water, tea and coffee are good everyday drinks for most people. Sugary drinks add a lot of sugar with little else, and fruit juice should be kept to a small glass.

Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kimchi and sauerkraut contain live bacteria. Early research suggests that they may help the gut, but the evidence is still young, so they are a tasty extra rather than a cure.

Some studies suggest that people who eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains are less likely to feel depressed. Mr Bashir says that this is an area of active research, so it is a hope and not a promise.

Lena sees shelves full of vitamin pills and powders and asks if she needs them. Mr Bashir says that, for most healthy people, a varied diet works better than pills, although some people do need a particular supplement.
Mr Bashir reminds Lena that food is only one part of a healthy life. Sleep, regular movement, not smoking and good friends all matter too, and nobody controls every part of their health.
A magazine advertises a detox tea that promises to wash poisons from the body. Mr Bashir laughs, because the liver and kidneys already do that job, and no tea has been shown to do it better.
Lena's niece Maya refuses broccoli, so Lena asks Mr Bashir for advice. He says that children often need to try a new food many times before they like it, so patience works better than pressure.
In October, Lena keeps a diary for a second week and compares it with the first. She now eats far more vegetables, beans and whole grains, and she has not given up the foods that she loves.

Mr Bashir tells Lena that a good diet does not replace regular health checks. Blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar can only be measured by a professional, and many problems give no early signs.

Many studies of Mediterranean-style and other plant-rich diets link them with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers. These links are not guarantees, but they are consistent and they come from many different kinds of research.
Mr Bashir says that big plans often fail, while small habits often last. He suggests that Lena try one new plant-based meal each week, and keep the ones she really enjoys.
In December, Lena invites her friends and Mr Bashir to dinner. She serves lentil stew, roasted vegetables and baked apples with nuts, and everyone asks for the recipes.
This book gives general information about eating more plants, and it is not medical advice. If you have a health condition or a special diet, please talk to a doctor or a dietitian first.
C1C2: On a grey January evening, Lena looked into her fridge, found nothing but ready meals and a wilting lettuce, and decided that something had to change. Next door lived Mr Bashir, a retired dietitian with a vegetable patch and a gift for explaining complicated things simply. When she asked for advice over the garden fence, he smiled, put down his spade and said that he had been waiting years for someone to ask.

Mr Bashir's first lesson is that the goal is more, not only: nobody has to give up everything else overnight. Plants, he says, means vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, whole grains, nuts and seeds, a wide family of foods that is much bigger than a salad. Most healthy eating patterns around the world, he adds, put these foods at the centre of the plate and leave other things at the edges.

Many national food guides, Mr Bashir tells her, suggest a plate that is about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein, with a little healthy oil. The pictures differ from country to country, but the general shape is much the same. He sketches it on a paper napkin, and Lena sticks it to the fridge like a map of a country she has not yet visited.

Before changing anything, Mr Bashir suggests, it is wise to see what one actually eats, so Lena keeps a food diary for a week. Reading it back, she notices that most of her meals are built around bread, pasta and cheese, with vegetables appearing as a garnish or not at all. It is an honest picture, and she finds it more interesting than embarrassing, because it shows exactly where to begin.

The World Health Organization advises eating at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, which works out at about five portions of 80 grams each. Surveys in many countries show that most adults fall short of this modest target, and Mr Bashir finds the fact more worrying than surprising. Potatoes do not count, he adds, although they are a perfectly good food in their own right.

Fibre is the tough, indigestible part of plant foods, found in vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds, and it is not found in meat, fish, eggs or dairy products. Some national guidelines, such as those of the United Kingdom, advise adults to eat about thirty grams of it a day, yet the average adult eats considerably less. Lena counts the fibre in her typical day and discovers, with a small groan, that she is nowhere near the target.

Fibre, Mr Bashir explains, does several useful things at once: it keeps the bowels moving, and it helps people to feel full for longer. In its soluble form, found in oats, beans and fruit, it can also help to lower cholesterol in the blood, and it is the favourite food of the bacteria that live in the large intestine. Diets rich in fibre are linked in many studies with a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer, although a link, he is careful to say, is not the same as proof.

The large intestine is home to trillions of microbes, mostly bacteria, which together make up what scientists call the gut microbiome. When they ferment fibre, they produce short-chain fatty acids, substances that seem to nourish the cells lining the gut and may influence the body in other ways. The field is young and exciting, Mr Bashir warns, and anyone who promises simple miracles from it is running far ahead of the evidence.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas, which together are called pulses or legumes, are among the cheapest and most useful foods in the world, packed with both fibre and protein. Tinned ones need no preparation beyond a rinse, while dried ones cost even less and keep for years in a cupboard. Lena, who had always thought of beans as something for camping trips, begins to see her kitchen shelves differently.

For her first plant-based supper, Lena simmers red lentils with onion, garlic, cumin and a squeeze of lemon, and the kitchen fills with a smell that she finds unexpectedly comforting. Mr Bashir, tasting a spoonful over the fence, approves and adds a safety note: dried red kidney beans contain a natural toxin and must be soaked and then boiled hard for at least ten minutes before they are eaten. Lentils, fortunately, are far more forgiving and need no soaking at all, which is one more reason to begin with them.

After a few days of bean-heavy meals, Lena discovers the best-known side effect of a plant-rich diet, which is a great deal of wind. Mr Bashir, quite unembarrassed, explains that the bacteria are simply fermenting the extra fibre, and that most people's guts adapt within a few weeks if the change is made gradually. He suggests small portions at first, plenty of water and patience, and he adds that anyone with persistent stomach trouble should ask a doctor.

A whole grain still has all of its parts, including the outer bran and the germ, which are rich in fibre, vitamins and minerals, whereas refined grains such as white flour have lost most of them in milling. Lena begins to swap one meal at a time, choosing wholemeal bread, brown rice, barley and oats in place of their paler cousins. The change in taste, she finds, is smaller than she feared, and the change in how long she feels full is larger than she expected.

Her new breakfast is a bowl of porridge, topped with chopped fruit, a few nuts and a spoonful of seeds, and it costs less than the cereal she used to buy. Large studies in many countries link a diet rich in whole grains with a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, although they cannot show that grains alone are the cause. Mr Bashir smiles, because that last phrase is exactly the point he has been waiting to make.

Many food studies, Mr Bashir explains, are observational: they follow large groups of people for years, record what they eat and note who becomes ill. People who eat plenty of whole plant foods tend also to smoke less and exercise more, so scientists work hard to adjust for such differences, and they test the most promising ideas in controlled trials as well. No single study settles a question, he says, but when many different kinds of evidence point the same way, it is wise to take notice.

Red tomatoes, orange carrots, green spinach and purple cabbage all owe their colours to different natural pigments, and many of these pigments seem to have their own effects in the body. Mr Bashir cautions, however, that the point is variety rather than any single wonder-food, and that the word superfood is mostly a marketing idea. Lena, standing at the market stall, decides to buy something of a colour that she has not bought for weeks.

Spinach, kale, chard and cabbage are rich in fibre, folate, vitamin K and a host of other plant compounds, and they cost very little when they are in season. There is one important caution, which Mr Bashir gives without being asked: vitamin K affects the blood-thinning medicine warfarin. Anyone who takes it should ask their doctor before making a large change to their intake of leafy greens, since general advice is never a substitute for advice from someone who knows their history.

Boiling vegetables for a long time, Mr Bashir explains, can leave some of their vitamins in the water, while steaming, roasting and quick stir-frying keep more of them in the food. Cooking is not always a loss, however, since heat helps the body to take up some compounds, such as the lycopene in tomatoes and the beta-carotene in carrots. Lena roasts a tray of peppers, onions and courgettes with olive oil and herbs, and discovers that vegetables can taste like a treat.

Fresh is not always best, Mr Bashir tells her, because frozen vegetables are usually picked and frozen within hours, and they often keep their nutrients as well as fresh ones that have spent days in transport and storage. Tinned tomatoes, beans and chickpeas, which are cooked in the can, are similarly useful, especially if the label shows no added salt or sugar. A freezer drawer full of peas, spinach and mixed vegetables, he says, is a small insurance policy against takeaway menus.

An orange and a glass of orange juice are not the same food, Mr Bashir points out, because pressing the fruit removes most of its fibre and leaves the sugar free to be absorbed quickly. The World Health Organization advises that free sugars, a group that includes those in fruit juice, honey and syrups as well as in sweets, should make up less than ten percent of a person's daily energy. Lena keeps a bowl of whole fruit on the table, and finds that she reaches for it more often than for biscuits.

Walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts and seeds such as pumpkin and flax supply healthy unsaturated fats, protein, fibre and minerals, and many studies link a small daily handful, about thirty grams, with a lower risk of heart disease. Because nuts are rich in energy, a handful is enough, and Lena finds that it works well scattered over porridge or salads. Mr Bashir reminds her that nut allergies can be serious, so anyone who is sensitive, or who lives with young children, should follow medical advice.

Not all fats behave alike, Mr Bashir says: most plant oils, such as olive and rapeseed oil, are rich in unsaturated fats, whereas butter, cream and fatty meats contain more saturated fat. Health bodies in many countries advise replacing part of the saturated fat in the diet with unsaturated fat, which is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. Coconut and palm oils, though they come from plants, are high in saturated fat, so the word plant on a label does not settle the matter.

In 2015, the cancer research agency of the World Health Organization placed processed meats, such as bacon, ham and sausages, in its highest evidence category as a cause of bowel cancer, and it called red meat a probable cause. Mr Bashir is careful to explain that such a classification describes how strong the evidence is, not how large the risk is, and that the risk from an occasional serving is small. His practical advice is modest: eat less processed meat, keep red meat for occasional meals, and let beans, vegetables, fish or eggs do more of the work.

Protein is found in a great many plant foods, among them beans, lentils, tofu, nuts, seeds and even whole grains, and the old belief that these must be carefully combined at every meal has long been set aside. A varied diet over the course of a day, dietitians now agree, provides all the building blocks that the body needs. Lena, who had always imagined a plate without meat as a plate without protein, is both relieved and slightly embarrassed.

Tofu and tempeh, both made from soya beans, are old foods in many Asian kitchens, and they take on the flavour of whatever they are cooked with. The meat substitutes in supermarket freezers are a different matter, Mr Bashir says, since they range from simple and nutritious to heavily processed and salty, so the label is worth reading. As for soya itself, current evidence suggests that moderate amounts are safe, and may be useful, for most people.

Ultra-processed foods, such as many fizzy drinks, packaged snacks and ready meals, are industrial products made from ingredients and additives that rarely appear in a home kitchen. Many large studies link diets high in them with weight gain and poorer health, although it is still debated whether the cause is the processing itself or the sugar, salt and fat that so often come with it. Mr Bashir does not ask Lena to give up tinned beans or wholemeal bread, only to notice what is in her basket and to let whole foods fill most of her plate.

Too much salt raises blood pressure in many people, and the World Health Organization advises that adults eat less than five grams of it a day, roughly one level teaspoon, which is less than most people actually consume. Much of the salt we eat is hidden in bread, sauces, soups and processed foods rather than added at the table, so Lena begins to check labels. Her answer to the problem is a change of habit rather than a sacrifice, since fresh herbs, spices, lemon juice and garlic can make a dish taste vivid with hardly any salt at all.

Sugar hides in many foods that do not taste especially sweet, from pasta sauces and soups to breakfast cereals and flavoured yoghurts, and the label may list it under a dozen different names. Lena discovers that cooking from simple ingredients reduces the problem almost without effort, because a lentil or a carrot arrives with no added sugar at all. A little sweetness is not a crime, Mr Bashir says, but it is worth knowing where it is coming from.

By midsummer, Lena has turned a neglected corner of the garden into a patch of beans, salad leaves, tomatoes and herbs, with Mr Bashir leaning on the fence and offering advice that she sometimes follows. Food that she has grown herself tastes remarkable, and she finds that she is more willing to eat what she has watched grow. The gardening also gets her outdoors and moving, which is a useful benefit that has nothing to do with vegetables.

When Lena adds up her receipts for the month, she discovers with real pleasure that her new way of eating costs less than the old. Dried beans, lentils, oats, rice and seasonal vegetables are among the cheapest foods in any shop, while meat, fish and branded convenience foods, which once filled her trolley, were the real expense. Mr Bashir nods, since he has long held that a healthy diet should not be a luxury, and he shares his favourite tricks for stretching a budget.

Planning, Mr Bashir says, is the quiet secret of a good diet, and Lena starts to sketch out a week of meals every Sunday before writing a shopping list. She buys fewer impulse snacks, wastes less food and always keeps a supply of tinned beans, frozen vegetables, oats and rice in reserve for evenings when she is too tired to think. The list is plain and unglamorous, but it turns good intentions into groceries, and groceries into dinner.

On Sunday afternoons, Lena has discovered the pleasure of batch cooking: a large pot of soup, stew or curry is made once, divided into boxes and frozen for the weeks ahead. On a tired Wednesday evening she then needs only a saucepan and ten minutes, and the temptation of the takeaway menu loses much of its power. Mr Bashir, who has done this for decades, calls it the best present one can give one's future self.

Plain beans and boiled vegetables, Lena learns, are dull only until they meet a well-stocked spice shelf, and her cooking improves the moment she begins to use cumin, smoked paprika, ginger, turmeric and fresh coriander. Many of the world's great cuisines, Mr Bashir points out, grew up around exactly this skill, making modest plant foods delicious through flavour rather than expense. Each week she tries one new spice, and each week the kitchen smells a little more interesting.

At her brother Jonas's birthday barbecue, Lena fills her plate with vegetable skewers, bean salad and corn, takes a small piece of the grilled chicken to be polite, and discovers that nobody is watching her at all. Mr Bashir had warned her that all-or-nothing rules are a poor plan, because the best diet is the one that a person can enjoy and keep for years. Food, he says, is also about friends, memory and pleasure, and a healthy way of eating has room for all three.

Vitamin B12 is made by bacteria and found naturally in meat, fish, eggs and dairy foods, but not reliably in plants, so it is the one nutrient that every fully plant-based eater must plan for. Fortified foods, such as some plant milks and cereals, or a supplement, can supply it, and Mr Bashir tells Lena that the right amount is a question for a doctor or a registered dietitian. Because Lena still eats eggs and dairy foods, she is not at particular risk, but he wants her to know the facts before she meets a friend who is.

Anyone who eats little or no animal food, Mr Bashir says, should also pay attention to iron, calcium, iodine, vitamin D and omega-3 fats, all of which are easier to get from a varied plate than from a narrow one. Beans, leafy greens, nuts and fortified plant milks help with several of these, and vitamin C from fruit helps the body to take in the iron from plants. In countries with little winter sun, vitamin D is a concern for almost everyone, whatever they eat, and many health bodies advise a supplement in the darker months.

Babies, young children, pregnant women, older people and anyone with a medical condition may have particular nutritional needs, Mr Bashir stresses, and for them a big change of diet should be made with professional advice. People with kidney disease, for example, are sometimes told to limit foods that are rich in potassium and phosphorus, including some beans, nuts and leafy greens, which shows why a general rule can be wrong for a particular person. Lena notes that her own plan is gentle, and that his message is not to fear plants but to ask an expert when in doubt.

Vegetables, fruit and beans are bulky and watery, so they fill the stomach while supplying relatively little energy for their weight, which is one reason why plant-rich diets often leave people satisfied. For most adults this is a pleasant side effect, Mr Bashir says, but growing children, very active people and anyone who loses weight unintentionally may need to add energy-dense foods such as nuts, seeds, oils and whole grains. Lena, who now eats more food than before and is no hungrier, finds that the arithmetic of her plate has quietly changed.

Water remains the simplest and best everyday drink, Mr Bashir says, and unsweetened tea and coffee, taken in moderation, are fine for most people and may even bring some small benefits. Sugary soft drinks, on the other hand, supply a great deal of sugar and almost nothing else, and fruit juice is best kept to a small glass. Lena puts a jug of water with lemon and mint on the table, and finds that the whole household drinks more of it.

Yoghurt, kimchi, sauerkraut and other fermented foods contain live bacteria, and there is some early evidence that eating them regularly may support the gut and the body's defences. Mr Bashir shares the enthusiasm but not the exaggeration, because the studies are still few and small, and the bacteria in different foods are not interchangeable. They are a tasty extra, he says, rather than a cure, and Lena adds a spoonful of sauerkraut to her lunch simply because she enjoys the sharp taste.

Several studies have found that people who eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains are less likely to report feeling depressed. Mr Bashir is quick to point out that such links may partly reflect other differences in people's lives, and that research into food and mood is active but young. He describes it as a hope rather than a promise, and anyone who feels low for weeks on end, he adds, should speak to a doctor rather than rely on a menu.

Standing in front of a shelf of vitamin pills and powders, Lena asks Mr Bashir whether she ought to be buying any of them. For most healthy people, he answers, a varied diet is the better investment, because foods contain fibre and countless compounds that a tablet cannot copy, and trials of general multivitamins have not shown clear protection against disease. Some people do need a particular supplement, such as vitamin B12 or vitamin D, but that is a decision to make with a doctor or dietitian rather than with a shop display.

Food is only one part of a healthy life, Mr Bashir reminds her, and a perfect diet cannot make up for poor sleep, a lack of movement, smoking or a life with no friends in it. Genes, luck and circumstances play a part too, which means that nobody controls every piece of their own health, and nobody should feel guilty about the pieces that they do not. Lena takes this as a relief, and she goes for a long walk with a friend that evening.

A glossy magazine advertises a detox tea that promises to wash the poisons out of the body in seven days, and Mr Bashir, reading it over the fence, laughs until he has to wipe his glasses. The liver and the kidneys, he explains, are already excellent at clearing waste, and there is no good evidence that any tea or juice cleanse does the job better. The best detox plan, in his dry opinion, is the plain one of eating more plants and drinking enough water.

Lena's young niece Maya pushes away every green thing on her plate, and Lena, with all her new enthusiasm, asks Mr Bashir how to win the argument. He answers that it is not an argument at all, because children often need to meet a new food again and again, sometimes ten times or more, before they accept it. Calm repetition, small portions and good examples work far better than pressure, he says, and Maya is soon crunching raw carrot sticks with a dip.

In October, Lena keeps her food diary for a second week and lays it beside the one she wrote in January, and the difference is plain to see. Vegetables, beans, oats and fruit now fill the page, and the ready meals have almost vanished, although a slice of cake and a plate of cheese still appear on Sundays. She does not claim to feel transformed, but she notices that she cooks more, spends less and no longer thinks of eating well as a punishment.

A good diet is no replacement for regular health checks, Mr Bashir insists, because conditions such as high blood pressure and raised blood sugar cause no symptoms early on and can be found only by measuring. Lena books an appointment with her doctor, partly out of curiosity and partly because she has promised him. The visit is quick and unremarkable, which, as the nurse says with a smile, is exactly what one hopes for.

Over many years, studies of Mediterranean-style diets and of other eating patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains and nuts have repeatedly linked them with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers. None of this is a guarantee for any single person, Mr Bashir cautions, and the details of the best diet are still argued over by scientists, who rarely agree about the small print. What impresses him is the consistency of the picture, which has held for decades across different countries and different kinds of research.

Big plans collapse, Mr Bashir says, while small habits tend to survive, so he advises anyone who wants to eat more plants to add just one new meal a week. They should keep only the ones that they truly enjoy, and after a year the gentle method adds up to dozens of new recipes, without a single dramatic resolution or a single day of misery. Lena sticks a calendar to the fridge and puts a small green tick on every Monday.

In December, Lena invites her friends and Mr Bashir to dinner, and she serves a rich lentil stew, a tray of roasted winter vegetables and baked apples stuffed with nuts and cinnamon. Nobody remarks that the meal is plant-based until the plates are empty, at which point her brother Jonas asks for seconds and the recipes. It is exactly the kind of evening that she could not have imagined in January, and she suspects that it is the best advertisement for her new way of eating.

As the year ends, Lena and Mr Bashir sit over a pot of tea and agree that the best change is the one that lasts, and that eating more plants is a direction rather than a test. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy or a special diet should ask a doctor or a registered dietitian before making changes. For everyone else, the next step is small and delicious: put one more plant on tomorrow's plate.
